body: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway now supports the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream APIs on its inference endpoint, along with model fallback routing for inference traffic. With InvokeModel support, you can point your existing Amazon Bedrock SDK integration at the gateway and reach any model provider through one governed endpoint, without rewriting client code for each provider. With model fallback, the gateway automatically routes a request to an alternative model or provider when the primary destination is throttled, out of capacity, or unreachable, so your agents stay available without each client implementing its own retry logic. For fallback routing, you define an ordered chain of alternative destinations in a gateway rule, along with the conditions that trigger a switch, such as throttling, server errors, or response timeouts. A built-in circuit breaker skips destinations that are currently failing, so requests reach a healthy destination faster and you avoid added latency for failed attempts. Fallback routing happens behind the scenes, which means you send one request and receive one response, regardless of the internal trial and error on a given request. These features are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway is available (except those in China). To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway User Guide .

title: Amazon Connect Customer now enables you to use flow modules in agentic CX designer
body: Amazon Connect Customer now enables you to use flow modules as data requests in agentic CX designer, so you can build and apply reusable logic across your customer experience flows. You can run a flow module at a fixed step in a conversation with a Data request node, or give it to a Generative journey as a tool to call when the conversation needs it. With this launch, you can use flow modules to update customer profiles and cases, create tasks, look up data tables, send an SMS confirmation, or check hours of operation and staffing before escalating to a human agent. You can also retrieve data that sits inside a private network, such as core banking, policy, or claims systems. For example, a flow module can invoke an AWS Lambda function in your VPC to return an account balance or claim status in the middle of an interaction. This feature is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London). To learn more, refer to Data requests and Flow modules in the Connect Customer documentation. To learn more about Amazon Connect Customer, an agentic AI solution that helps enterprises deliver exceptional customer experiences, visit the Amazon Connect Customer website .

title: GLM 5.3 by Z.ai is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock
body: Amazon Bedrock now supports GLM 5.3 from Z.ai, giving you a powerful new option for agentic coding and long-horizon software engineering work. Customers using GLM 5.3 on Amazon Bedrock have access to the latest open weight model with the AWS security and compliance posture. GLM 5.3 is Z.ai’s flagship model, a mixture-of-experts architecture with 753B total parameters and roughly 40B active per token, built on the same base model as GLM 5.2 with all improvements driven by scaled post-training. It combines a 1-million-token context window with up to 128K output tokens, and reasoning is always enabled with selectable effort levels so you can trade latency and token consumption against task performance. Bedrock support for GLM 5.3 includes explicit prompt caching with cache points on system prompts and messages, helping you reduce latency and input costs when reusing context across model calls. GLM 5.3 is available to eligible enterprise customers, and is accessible through the US and Global cross-Region inference profiles. To get started with GLM 5.3, you can access the model in the Amazon Bedrock console or programmatically through supported Amazon Bedrock APIs. For information about supported AWS Regions , endpoints, APIs, features, inference profiles and pricing, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation . To learn more, read the launch blog post .

title: Amazon Connect Customer Global Resiliency now supports persistent chat across linked AWS Regions
body: Amazon Connect Customer Global Resiliency now provides customers a mechanism to deliver long, persistent chat experiences across linked AWS Regions. With this capability, end users can resume previous conversations with full context, metadata, and transcripts carried over across Regions, eliminating the need for end users to repeat information and allowing agents to provide personalized service with access to the entire conversation history across AWS Regions. For example, an end user can start a chat in US-East (N. Virginia) and later come back to it in the linked US-West (Oregon) Region, continuing the same conversation with an agent with full conversation history and chat attachment. To adopt this capability, onboard to Global routing . This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Connect Customer Global Resiliency is supported. To learn more, visit Amazon Connect Customer Admin Guide .

title: Amazon DCV releases version 2026.0 with RHEL 10 support and new clients
body: Amazon DCV 2026.0 is now available, adding support for RHEL 10, Rocky Linux 10, CentOS 10, and Ubuntu 26.04 along with a new macOS client and updated Windows and Linux clients. Amazon DCV is a high-performance remote display protocol that enables customers to securely access remote desktops and application sessions across Windows, Linux, and macOS. Amazon DCV 2026.0 includes the following key features and improvements: Support for RHEL 10, Rocky Linux 10, CentOS 10, and Ubuntu 26.04, with Linux hosts and sessions running on the modern Wayland display server A new macOS client with gamepad support, and updated Windows and Linux clients URL redirection on Windows hosts, so configured links opened in a remote session launch in the local browser on the client device Printer preferences redirection on Windows, giving remote sessions access to client-side printer settings Performance improvements, including H.264 frame slice support and slice-based multithreaded decoding on the Linux and macOS clients for lower latency Support for new macOS server versions on Amazon EC2 For more information about the new features and enhancements in Amazon DCV 2026.0, see the release notes or visit the Amazon DCV webpage to learn more and get started.

title: Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS)
body: Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS), enabling you to run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU. GPU sharing helps you increase GPU utilization and reduce infrastructure costs for workloads that use only part of a GPU's capacity, such as small-model inference, AV/ADAS simulations, embedding generation, and multi-model serving. With GPU sharing, you can pack more workloads onto each GPU instance without changing your application code. You define the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally set a maximum share of GPU compute, and Amazon ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale and deploy. GPU sharing is supported on Amazon ECS Managed Instances and Amazon ECS on Amazon EC2. On Amazon ECS Managed Instances, Amazon ECS also monitors the MPS control daemon that enables sharing on each instance. If the daemon stops or becomes unhealthy, Amazon ECS automatically replaces the instance and moves your tasks to healthy capacity, so your GPU workloads keep running without manual intervention. To get started, use the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, or other infrastructure-as-code tools to create a capacity provider with NVIDIA GPU instances, set the GPU sharing strategy and memory in the container definition of your task definition, and create a service on that capacity provider. This capability is available in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions . To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS GPU sharing documentation .

title: Amazon EKS Dashboard now provides fleet-wide visibility into certificate authority (CA) rotation
body: Today, Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) announces certificate authority (CA) rotation visibility in the Amazon EKS Dashboard, giving you a consolidated view of CA rotation across your clusters. The Amazon EKS Dashboard already provides centralized visibility into your clusters across AWS Regions and accounts, and it now includes CA rotation, so you can see where action is needed without checking each cluster individually. Each Amazon EKS cluster has its own CA, and clusters created since 2018 have CAs with a 10-year validity period that are now approaching the point where rotation activities should begin. In the EKS Dashboard, you can now see your clusters and their CA rotation status, which clusters have CAs approaching expiration, and upcoming automated rotation events, so platform teams who operate many clusters can prioritize action across their fleet from one place. The Amazon EKS Dashboard aggregates data across your accounts and Regions through AWS Organizations, so you enable trusted access for the dashboard in your organization’s management account to use this capability. You view the dashboard from the US East region (us-east-1), and it is available at no additional cost. CA rotation support extends to all commercial AWS Regions, and the dashboard brings that rotation status together in one fleet-wide view. To learn more, see the Amazon EKS documentation .

title: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey now supports OpenTelemetry metrics and detailed monitoring
body: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey now publishes OpenTelemetry metrics to Amazon CloudWatch for your node-based clusters, and each metric carries attributes you can filter and aggregate on with Prometheus Query Language (PromQL) expressions. ElastiCache now offers two monitoring modes. Standard monitoring, the existing experience, continues to publish CloudWatch Metrics (Classic) every 60 seconds and now also publishes a core set of OpenTelemetry metrics at the same interval at no additional charge. Detailed monitoring, the new mode, lets you select from the full set of OpenTelemetry metrics and publish them every 15 seconds. With OpenTelemetry metrics, you can detect any node in a cluster nearing its connection limit, break errors down by type during an incident, or forecast if a node will run out of memory. You can run these queries in CloudWatch and Grafana, keeping PromQL skills your team already has. With detailed monitoring, you can balance diagnostic depth and cost, with 15-second metrics enabling detection of short-lived events like latency spikes. The core set of OpenTelemetry metrics also powers ElastiCache Insights , a pre-built dashboard in Amazon CloudWatch. To get started, open the Metrics tab for a cluster in the Amazon ElastiCache console , select Detailed, and choose Configure detailed metrics. OpenTelemetry metrics and detailed monitoring are available for node-based Valkey clusters in all AWS Regions where Amazon CloudWatch supports OpenTelemetry metrics. There is no additional charge from ElastiCache for detailed monitoring. CloudWatch pricing for OpenTelemetry metrics applies to the detailed monitoring metrics you select, alarms you create, and PromQL API queries you run. To learn more, see Monitoring ElastiCache with OpenTelemetry metrics in the Amazon ElastiCache User Guide.

title: Amazon GameLift Servers adds CPU burstability for container fleets
body: Amazon GameLift Servers now supports CPU burstability for container fleets, giving game developers greater flexibility in how compute resources are allocated and consumed at runtime. Previously, container fleets relied on a fixed CPU value that simultaneously controlled both container packing density and imposed a hard runtime cap. This dual constraint forced developers to choose between efficient resource utilization and maintaining performance headroom for their game server workloads. Game server workloads are inherently bursty, CPU demand stays low during most of a match but spikes sharply during physics calculations, AI processing, or collision detection. With CPU burstability, developers can now pack containers based on typical CPU needs while still allowing game server processes to burst into available idle instance CPU during peak demand moments. This opt-in feature is configured per container group definition, supports high-density deployments without sacrificing peak performance, and is included at no additional cost as part of standard container fleet pricing. CPU burstability for Amazon GameLift Servers container fleets is available in all AWS Regions where container fleets are supported, excluding China Regions. To learn more about CPU burstability for Amazon GameLift Servers container fleets, visit the Amazon GameLift Servers Developer Guide or explore the Amazon GameLift Servers product page .

title: Amazon MSK Connect now supports pausing and resuming connectors
body: Amazon MSK Connect (Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka Connect) now supports pausing and resuming connectors, letting you temporarily pause a connector from processing records and resume it later. This is useful when you need to stop data flow during maintenance on a source database or a sink target, or to pause processing while you investigate an upstream or downstream issue. Amazon MSK Connect is a fully managed service that allows you to deploy, monitor, and scale Apache Kafka Connect connectors with Amazon MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka). Previously, pausing a connector meant deleting it and recreating it - a more disruptive operation, adding risk and operational overhead. With this launch, you can pause a running connector and resume it in place when you are ready — a paused connector keeps its configuration, capacity settings, and committed offsets, and its tasks continue processing from the offsets they last committed when you resume. This capability is available at no additional cost through the Amazon MSK Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDK, and AWS CDK in all AWS Regions where Amazon MSK Connect is available. To learn more, visit the Amazon MSK Connect documentation . To get started, visit the Amazon MSK Console .

title: Amazon OpenSearch Service introduces intelligent ingestion for logs and documents in Amazon S3
body: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless now offers intelligent ingestion, a fully managed feature that turns logs and documents stored in Amazon S3 into searchable content in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless (NextGen) collections . With intelligent ingestion, you can set up ingestion with a few clicks in the AWS Management Console or a single API call, with no ingestion infrastructure to manage. Intelligent ingestion supports observability logs and structured data in JSON, NDJSON, and JSON array formats, and unstructured files in PDF, Word, plain text, and Markdown formats. You choose an S3 source and a collection index, and intelligent ingestion handles the rest. It automatically detects data types, parses documents, describes images, chunks text, generates vector embeddings, and indexes the results. You don't need to manage ingestion or document-processing infrastructure, or size capacity in advance. Use ingestion jobs for one-time loads such as migrations and backfills, or ingestion streams to keep an index in sync as new objects arrive in your bucket. Capacity scales with your workload up to the collection's configured limit, and you pay only for active processing. Source S3 buckets can be in the same AWS account as the collection or in a different account. For logs and structured data, intelligent ingestion applies transformations and optionally adds embeddings, with no pipeline code. For unstructured data, it parses PDF, Word, plain text, and Markdown files while keeping headings, reading order, and tables intact, so the content lands in an index ready for semantic and hybrid search. When documents contain charts, diagrams, screenshots, or photos, a vision-language model generates text descriptions that are indexed with the surrounding content, making visual information searchable too. Intelligent ingestion is available today for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless (NextGen) collections, with Amazon S3 as the source, in seven AWS Regions. To get started, open the Amazon OpenSearch Service console, choose your collection, and select the Ingestion tab. To learn more, see Intelligent ingestion in the Amazon OpenSearch Service Developer Guide. For pricing, see Amazon OpenSearch Service pricing .

title: Amazon Quick now supports brand templates for on-brand presentations and documents
body: Starting today, you can upload brand templates in Amazon Quick, allowing you to create presentations and documents that match your approved visual identity. Brand managers set up a template once and everyone gets on-brand output, without hunting for the right file in each chat. Brand managers upload PowerPoint or Word templates, or pull them from a connected file store such as SharePoint. Quick extracts the colors, fonts, logos, layouts and brand rules from each file. A brand manager reviews and edits what Quick found before publishing it to the whole organization. Quick also follows a template's rules as it creates new assets. If a request breaks a rule, Quick explains why and suggests an on-brand alternative. For each task, Quick picks the best-fit template based on guidance the brand manager writes. Users can still choose a different template. Administrators decide who can create and publish brand templates using custom permissions, ensuring that only the proper members of brand, marketing, or other approved teams can set visual standards. Brand assets are generally available today in the Amazon Quick desktop app. To learn more, see the Amazon Quick documentation, or create an account for free and start using Quick in minutes.

title: Amazon S3 Tables now support up to 100 table buckets per AWS Region in an AWS account
body: Amazon S3 Tables now support up to 100 table buckets per AWS Region in an AWS account, increased from 10. This allows you to create up to 1 million tables per AWS Region in an AWS account. With a higher table bucket allowance, you can create a separate table bucket for each dataset, workload, or team, and apply table bucket-level settings such as encryption, access policies, and replication to each. The higher quota applies by default to all accounts at no additional cost. S3 Tables deliver the first cloud object store with built-in Apache Iceberg support, and the easiest way to store tabular data at scale. S3 Tables perform continual table maintenance to automatically optimize query efficiency and storage cost over time, even as your data lake scales and evolves. The higher default quota is available in all AWS Regions where S3 Tables are available. If you need a quota beyond the default, you can request an increase through AWS Support. To learn more, visit the S3 Tables overview page , user guide , and quotas documentation .

title: Amazon WorkSpaces Core Managed Instances now supports ModifyVolume API
body: Amazon WorkSpaces Core Managed Instances now supports the ModifyVolume API, which lets you change volume size, volume type, IOPS, or throughput in place, without detaching the volume or restarting the instance. Previously, changing storage capacity or performance on a deployed managed instance required rebuilding it. With ModifyVolume, you can increase volume size up to 16,384 GiB, switch between supported Amazon EBS volume types, adjust IOPS for gp3, io1, and io2 volumes, and modify throughput for gp3 volumes. The API supports idempotency tokens to prevent duplicate changes, and you can track progress with the Amazon EC2 DescribeVolumesModifications operation. ModifyVolume is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon WorkSpaces Core Managed Instances is available. To get started, call ModifyVolume directly, or use it through your WorkSpaces Core partner solution once available. To learn more, see ModifyVolume in the WorkSpaces Instances API Reference and Limitations in the Amazon EBS User Guide, or visit WorkSpaces Core .

title: Amazon Aurora serverless now supports up to 384 ACUs
body: Amazon Aurora serverless now supports database capacity of up to 384 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) for Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition, a 50% increase from the previous maximum of 256 ACUs. Each ACU provides approximately 2 gibibytes (GiB) of memory with corresponding CPU and networking, so a single Aurora serverless database can now scale up to 768 GiB of memory. When the workload completes, Aurora serverless automatically scales down to zero. This makes Aurora serverless especially well-suited for agentic AI applications, which typically have bursts of activity, long idle windows, and unpredictable traffic patterns. Aurora serverless handles all of it automatically, scaling capacity with your agents, so you only pay for what you use. With 384 ACU support, customers can now use Aurora serverless for even more demanding workloads while continuing to scale down to zero when not in use, paying only for the capacity consumed. For new clusters, select a supported Aurora PostgreSQL engine version and set your maximum capacity up to 384 ACUs. For existing clusters on Platform Version 4, simply modify the cluster to update the maximum capacity setting (and the engine version if needed). There will be no downtime if your database is already on Platform Version 4. For existing clusters on older platform versions, upgrade to Platform Version 4 through a pending maintenance action. 384 ACU support is available for Aurora PostgreSQL versions 18.4, 17.10, 16.14, 15.18, and 14.23, running on Platform Version 4. To learn more, see Aurora serverless capacity in the Amazon Aurora User Guide. For pricing details and Region availability, visit Amazon Aurora Pricing . To get started, create or modify an Aurora serverless database in the AWS Management Console .

title: AWS announces TorchNeuron: Native PyTorch Support for AWS Trainium (Public Beta)
body: Today, AWS launched the public beta of TorchNeuron, an open source native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium. Trainium is a portfolio of AI chips designed to deliver high performance and cost efficiency for deep learning AI training and inference workloads. TorchNeuron enables AI scientists and researchers to experiment and build models with PyTorch natively on Trainium. With TorchNeuron, developers can enable their PyTorch code on Trainium simply by switching to .to('neuron') while maintaining full PyTorch compatibility with eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. TorchNeuron is available as open source through the TorchNeuron github repo for Amazon EC2 Trainium2 instances and Amazon EC2 Trainium3 instances. To learn more about TorchNeuron and AWS Trainium accelerators, visit the AWS Neuron page .

title: AWS Backup adds restore testing support for Amazon Redshift
body: AWS Backup restore testing now supports Amazon Redshift. Restore testing helps you automate and periodically run restore tests of your backups, so you can confirm that your Amazon Redshift backups restore successfully and measure how long the restores take. You can now include Amazon Redshift in your restore testing plans alongside other supported AWS resources across storage, compute, and database services. Restore testing plans automatically select recovery points, run restores on a schedule, and measure restore job completion time against your recovery time objectives (RTO). This helps you evaluate recovery readiness and meet regulatory and compliance requirements for disaster recovery and business continuity. To get started, create a restore testing plan and assign your Amazon Redshift resources by Amazon Resource Name (ARN) or tag. Choose whether each test restores the latest or a random eligible recovery point. Optionally, use restore testing validation to confirm the restored resource before AWS Backup deletes the test resources. This support is available in all AWS Regions where both restore testing and Amazon Redshift are supported by AWS Backup. You can use the AWS Backup console, AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or AWS SDKs. For a complete list of supported Regions and features, visit the AWS Backup documentation . To learn more about restore testing, visit the product page and pricing page .

title: AWS Cost Explorer, Budgets, and Dashboards now support Amazon Bedrock product attributes
body: AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, and AWS Cost Management Dashboards now let you analyze Amazon Bedrock costs by product attributes, a new dimension that breaks down Bedrock cost by model, model provider, inference type, and feature. In Cost Explorer and Dashboards, you can group and filter costs by these attributes. In Budgets, you can filter budgets by the same attributes. With this launch, finance and platform teams get a direct view of which models and workloads drive their Bedrock spend, and can act on it in the billing tools they already use. The attributes include model (such as Claude Sonnet 5 or Claude Haiku 4.5), model provider (such as Anthropic or Cohere), inference type (such as input tokens or output tokens), and feature (such as on-demand inference or reranker). You can combine product attributes with cost allocation tags on application inference profiles, projects, or workspaces to see which applications drive spend on each model, and with IAM principal tags to see which users or roles drive it. Group a month of Bedrock spend by model in Cost Explorer to find your most expensive models, build a dashboard widget that tracks cost per provider, or set a budget that alerts on spend for a single model. The Amazon Bedrock product attribute dimension is available today at no additional charge in all AWS Regions, excluding the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China (Beijing) and China (Ningxia) Regions. To learn more, see the user guides for Cost Explorer , Budgets , and Dashboards .

title: AWS Client VPN now supports device posture assessment
body: AWS Client VPN now supports device posture assessment, allowing you to verify that connecting user devices meet your security and compliance requirements before granting network access. This feature integrates with your existing device posture providers, so only trusted, compliant devices can access your AWS resources through Client VPN. Previously, Client VPN authenticated users through certificates, SAML, or Active Directory. With device posture assessment, you can now also integrate CrowdStrike , Jamf , or JumpCloud with Client VPN to automatically evaluate device security signals such as compliance scores, encryption status, and risk level before allowing a connection. You define these requirements using Cedar policies , giving you fine-grained control over which devices can connect. To help you author and validate these policies, Client VPN provides you a Test Policy tool that guides you through creating Cedar policies for your device posture requirements. This feature continuously re-evaluates device compliance during active sessions, and automatically disconnects a session if a device falls out of compliance, such as when risk score or security settings change. You can also use this feature in monitoring-only mode, which logs posture evaluation results without disconnecting sessions, so you can assess the impact of your policies before enforcing them. Device posture assessment works alongside your existing authorization rules to provide defense in depth. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Client VPN is available, at no additional cost. This feature requires AWS VPN Client version 6.2.0 or later. To learn more about Client VPN: Visit the AWS Client VPN product page Download the AWS VPN Client Read the AWS Client VPN administrator guide Read the AWS Client VPN user guide

title: AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing now supports continuous penetration testing integrated directly into your CI/CD pipeline
body: AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing now integrates continuous penetration testing directly into your CI/CD pipeline (public preview) AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing (formerly AWS Security Agent) already provides continuous, on-demand penetration testing without the need to contract third-party pentest vendors. Now, in public preview, Continuum for Penetration Testing shifts security testing even further left by integrating directly into your existing CI/CD systems, making penetration testing a deploy-time event. Development teams ship code daily, but even with on-demand penetration testing available, security validation often happens outside the deployment workflow. CI/CD integration closes this gap. Developers receive findings, including severity, affected endpoints, and remediation guidance, directly in pipeline output. Non-security changes complete with no meaningful delay, and the pipeline automatically re-tests and verifies fixes after remediation without requiring manual re-triggers. Getting started requires no security expertise. An auto-generated pipeline snippet can be pasted into any existing pipeline and is completable in under five minutes. Application context bootstraps automatically on the first run, with no prior full penetration test required. Continuous penetration testing is available today. To get started, visit our documentation .

title: AWS End User Messaging adds a guided wizard for RCS registration videos
body: Today, AWS End User Messaging adds a wizard that orchestrates the entire video capture for your RCS agent registration. RCS registrations in multiple countries, including the United States, require a screen recording that demonstrates your messaging experience. To record it, you have to send a specific sequence of messages to a test device, and until now you scripted those messages yourself, which easily introduced errors and made a mismatched or incomplete video one of the hardest parts of registering for RCS. The wizard now drives each step of the capture for you, sending the right messages in the right order, so you record a compliant video the first time and get your agent approved sooner. The wizard is on all RCS registration forms that require a video submission. To learn more and get started, see the AWS End User Messaging User Guide.

title: AWS Glue Data Catalog now supports table optimization, statistics, and crawlers for Apache Iceberg V3
body: AWS Glue Data Catalog now supports table optimization, statistics, and crawlers for Apache Iceberg Version 3 (V3) tables. With these new capabilities, you can automatically maintain V3 tables, optimize them for query performance, and discover them in Amazon S3. With table optimization, you can compact V3 tables using binpack, sort, or z-order strategies to improve query performance, and remove expired snapshots and orphan files to reduce storage costs. These optimizations support V3 data types, including variant, geospatial, and nanosecond-precision timestamps. You can also generate number of distinct values (NDV) statistics for V3 tables, which analytics engines use to plan queries efficiently. In addition, you can use Glue crawlers to discover V3 tables stored in Amazon S3 and register them in Glue Data Catalog, making them available to query with any V3-compatible engines. These capabilities are available for Iceberg V3 tables in all AWS Regions where Glue Data Catalog table optimization, statistics, and crawlers are available. To learn more, see Glue Optimization , Glue Statistics , and Glue crawlers in the Glue Developer Guide.

title: AWS HealthOmics introduces resource fallback order for Nextflow workflows
body: Today, AWS HealthOmics introduces the resource fallback directive for tasks in your Nextflow workflows, enabling you to define an ordered list of preferred accelerator types, including an option to fallback to CPU instances. Researchers and bioinformaticians can use this directive to reduce time spent diagnosing and resubmitting runs due to accelerator constraints and keep production workflows running. AWS HealthOmics is a HIPAA-eligible service that helps healthcare and life sciences customers accelerate scientific breakthroughs at scale with fully managed bioinformatics workflows. With resource fallback for Nextflow workflows, you can prioritize your preferred accelerator for your task. When your preferred accelerator is unavailable, HealthOmics automatically moves through your specified alternatives in the fallback without resubmission. Each accelerator profile has a configurable timeout, giving you control over how long HealthOmics searches for that accelerator before moving to the next. Shorter timeouts help you move quickly through the fallback order, while longer timeouts increase the probability of reserving your preferred accelerator. You can also include a CPU profile as a final fallback to increase the likelihood of your task reserving an instance. You can now use resource fallback for Nextflow workflows in all AWS HealthOmics Regions: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London), Israel (Tel Aviv), and Asia Pacific (Seoul, Singapore, Tokyo). To learn more, visit the advanced resource configuration and Nextflow specifics documentation.

title: AWS IAM Identity Center now supports network access controls for Identity Store
body: AWS IAM Identity Center helps you configure the single sign-on experience for your workforce to AWS accounts and applications. IAM Identity Center now supports network access controls for Identity Store, which stores your users and groups. You can restrict access to the Identity Store API and the SCIM API based on the network that requests originate from. Your custom applications and user provisioning workflows use the Identity Store API to manage and look up users and groups, and your external identity provider uses the SCIM API to synchronize users and groups. For the Identity Store API, you can require that requests arrive only through allowed VPC endpoints in your account or organization, or from specific source VPCs. For both APIs, you can allow requests only from specific IP ranges. Within the same configuration, you can apply different restrictions to each API. For example, you can require that Identity Store API requests arrive only through VPC endpoints, while allowing SCIM requests from your external identity provider's published IP ranges. Network access controls are optional and turned off by default. Requests that AWS services make on your behalf are exempt. You configure network access controls by using the Identity Store API through the AWS SDKs and AWS CLI. This capability is available in all AWS Regions where IAM Identity Center is offered. To learn more about IAM Identity Center, visit the product detail page . To get started with network access controls, see the Identity Store API Reference .

title: AWS Lambda announces Lambda Web Functions
body: AWS Lambda announces Lambda Web Functions, a new serverless compute primitive where your code handles HTTP requests directly. Your code listens on a port and handles requests as it would on any HTTP server. You use frameworks you already know, such as Express or Hono, with no adapters or custom configuration. This enables you to serve workloads such as AI inference endpoints, server-side rendered (SSR) web apps, streaming API endpoints, microservices, and webhooks. You pay for active CPU time and the memory your environment holds, not for idle CPU time your code spends waiting on databases or downstream services. With this launch, we are also renaming existing Lambda functions to Lambda Event Functions, a naming change only that requires no code changes or redeployments for your existing functions. Builders use Lambda to go from code to production quickly and without managing servers, across event-driven pipelines, request-response APIs, and data processing. As AI-driven development accelerates, they want to build locally and deploy with a familiar programming model and pay for workloads based on active CPU usage, while serving users with low latency. Lambda Web Functions delivers this. Today, Lambda Web Functions supports the Node.js runtime. A single warm execution environment can serve multiple concurrent requests, which reduces cold starts by orders of magnitude. You can stream results to clients incrementally with native HTTP streaming. You can create and configure Lambda Web Functions using the AWS Lambda API, Agent Toolkit for AWS , AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS CloudFormation, AWS SAM, AWS CDK, or the AWS SDKs. With multi-Region routing, you can deploy once and serve each request from the Region closest to the end user. Web Functions support Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connectivity, allowing your function to access resources that exist within a VPC. Lambda Web Functions is available today in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). For the current list, see the AWS Capabilities by Region page. To learn more, see the Lambda Web Functions developer guide . For pricing details, see AWS Lambda Pricing . To see Lambda Web Functions in action, see the AWS News Blog announcement .

title: AWS Private CA now provides detailed certificate issuance logs
body: AWS Private CA announces detailed certificate issuance logs, a new AWS CloudTrail service event that records the complete certificate content, issuing CA information, requester identity, and signing status for every issuance. You can use these events for compliance auditing, certificate inventory, algorithm migration tracking, and failed-issuance monitoring. Previously, the CloudTrail management event for the IssueCertificate API confirmed that the API call succeeded by providing a certificate ARN but did not capture the certificate content, information about the CA that signed it, or issuances that failed before signing. The new IssueCertificateDetails event captures the complete to-be-signed (TBS) certificate with all X.509 fields and extensions, plus convenience fields for the subject, issuer, serial number, validity period, template, and signing algorithm. Events are emitted for both successful and failed issuance, so pre-signing failures such as name constraints violations now produce a record with a failure explanation. Each event identifies the requester: the account and IAM principal for direct API callers, or the service principal for certificates issued through AWS Private CA connectors or integrated AWS services. In cross-account configurations, the event is delivered to the CA owner account. The event is delivered automatically as a CloudTrail management event, with no configuration or opt-in required and no additional cost beyond standard AWS CloudTrail pricing. Because it flows through CloudTrail, you can act on it in real time with Amazon EventBridge or query it in batch with Amazon Athena for certificate auditing, inventory, tracking, and monitoring. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Private CA is offered. To learn more, see the AWS Private CA User Guide .

title: AWS Transform announces Azure-to-AWS cloud-native code conversion
body: Today, AWS announced the general availability of application code conversion from Azure SDK to AWS SDK in AWS Transform, giving you an accelerated path to migrate Microsoft Azure cloud-native .NET applications to AWS. The AWS Transform .NET modernization agent identifies Azure service code and converts it to equivalent AWS service code. For example, an Azure Functions serverless function that uses Azure Cosmos DB can be converted to an AWS Lambda function that uses Amazon DynamoDB. AWS Transform discovers the Azure SDK in your submitted source code and presents the conversion options in the assessment report and modernization plan. You can accept the options provided or adjust them based on your preferences before running the modernization. AWS Transform then converts the identified Azure service code to the equivalent AWS SDK calls, and validates that the changes are incorporated into the transformed code. The feature supports conversion of Azure Functions to AWS Lambda functions, Azure Blob Storage to Amazon S3, and Azure Queue Storage to Amazon SQS, with Azure Cosmos DB to Amazon DynamoDB conversion available in preview. AWS Transform is available in eight AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Tokyo, Seoul, Sydney), Canada (Central), and Europe (Frankfurt, London). To learn more, see Convert cloud-native code to AWS in the AWS Transform User Guide.

title: AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Cloud WAN now support 1:1 NAT
body: AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Cloud WAN now provide managed one-to-one network address translation (NAT) directly on their attachments, through integration with Regional Private NAT Gateway. This enables customers to connect private networks that share the same IP address ranges without renumbering either network, deploying a NAT appliance, or writing return-traffic rules. Networks with overlapping Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) blocks have long been unable to communicate, a common blocker during mergers and acquisitions, when connecting partner networks over AWS Site-to-Site VPN, in multicloud connectivity, and when independently provisioned VPCs need to interconnect. Using this capability, customers can define address-translation rules on a AWS Transit Gateway or AWS Cloud WAN attachment, specifying the private IP range each source CIDR translates to, across Amazon VPC, AWS Site-to-Site VPN, AWS Direct Connect, and SD-WAN appliances connected through Transit Gateway Connect. Both services apply translation automatically in both directions, with no separate return-traffic rule and no NAT appliance to deploy. AWS operates, scales, and manages the NAT capability as part of the attachment. For example, if a customer acquires a business and both VPCs use 10.0.0.0/16, they translate one VPC's addresses to a non-overlapping range on its attachment and connect the networks immediately. Customers set it up in minutes using the AWS Management Console, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), AWS SDKs, and AWS CloudFormation, and monitor translated traffic through Amazon CloudWatch metrics and Amazon EventBridge events. AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Cloud WAN offer 1:1 NAT through Regional Private NAT Gateway in all AWS commercial regions where they operate. For full pricing details, see Amazon VPC pricing . To learn more, see the AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Cloud WAN product pages, and the AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Cloud WAN documentation.

title: Amazon Bedrock Advanced Prompt Optimization now supports prompt shortening
body: Amazon Bedrock Advanced Prompt Optimization now supports prompt shortening, an optional setting that reduces the length of your prompt while maintaining or improving your evaluation scores. Advanced Prompt Optimization optimizes prompts for any model on Amazon Bedrock against your own evaluation criteria. Until now, optimization focused on quality alone. Optimized prompts were often longer than the original. Longer prompts raise input token costs and can increase time to first token, which matters at scale and in latency-sensitive applications. When you turn on prompt shortening for a prompt template in your input dataset, the optimizer reduces the prompt's length. The optimized prompt is returned only when it is shorter than your original prompt and scores at least as high on your evaluation. Otherwise your original prompt is returned, so the setting never leaves you with a longer or lower-scoring prompt. Results include a compression ratio and the original and optimized token counts, in the output file and on the console results page. For example, a compression ratio of 0.7 means the optimized prompt uses 30% fewer tokens. Prompt shortening works with any evaluation method, including steering criteria, LLM-as-a-judge rubrics, and custom Lambda evaluators. Prompt shortening is available in all AWS Regions where Advanced Prompt Optimization is available. To get started, enable prompt shortening for a prompt template in your input dataset and create an optimization job as usual. To learn more, see Shorten prompts in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide, the Amazon Bedrock pricing page , and the Amazon Bedrock product page .

title: Amazon Braket now in scope for FedRAMP Class C
body: Amazon Braket is now in scope for FedRAMP Class C in AWS US Regions where Braket is available. The Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) is a US government-wide program that delivers a standard approach to the security assessment, authorization, and continuous monitoring of cloud products and services. With FedRAMP Class C authorization, government customers and the organizations that serve them can use Amazon Braket to explore quantum computing within an authorized boundary. The AWS-operated components of Braket, including the API and SDK, job orchestration and management, compilation, and result storage in Amazon S3, are within the FedRAMP-certified boundary, while quantum workloads execute on third-party Quantum Hardware Providers (QHPs) outside that boundary. All data sent to QHPs meets AWS' privacy and security requirements including removal of all personally identifiable information, data encryption in transit and at rest, and adherence to AWS' standard data retention and deletion policies. To learn more about FedRAMP, visit AWS FedRAMP services and the FedRAMP Marketplace. To learn more about Amazon Braket, visit the Braket product page and Getting Started on Braket resources. Regional Availability: US East (N. Virginia), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon)

title: Amazon Bedrock now offers Canada cross-Region inference for Claude Haiku 5.5
body: Amazon Bedrock now offers Canada cross-Region inference (CRIS) for Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5. Customers with strict data residency requirements can now keep inference processing entirely within Canada. Canada CRIS routes requests only between ca-central-1 (Canada Central) and ca-west-1 (Canada West, Calgary). This helps organizations in financial services, healthcare, the public sector, and other regulated industries meet federal and provincial data residency requirements. Canada CRIS adds to the inference options already available to customers in Canada. US CRIS and global CRIS remain fully supported for Claude Haiku 5.5. Both route requests across a broader set of AWS Regions, and global CRIS also offers cost savings, which makes these options a good fit for workloads that don't require inference processing to stay in Canada. Canada CRIS is designated as an inference profile with limited model selection. Future models and model versions might not be released for this profile. We recommend Canada CRIS for workloads that must keep inference processing within Canada. For more details, see Inference profiles with limited model selection in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. For the most current information about model availability in each Region, see Regional availability by models in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. To get started with Claude models on Amazon Bedrock, visit the Amazon Bedrock console.

title: Amazon CloudFront announces dual-stack support for VPC origins
body: Amazon CloudFront now supports end-to-end IPv6 delivery to origins inside your Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), with the new dual-stack VPC origins. With VPC origins, customers keep their Application Load Balancers (ALB), Network Load Balancers (NLB), and EC2 instances in private subnets that only their CloudFront distributions can reach. With dual-stack support, customers can now send IPv6 traffic all the way to these private origins to meet their IPv6 architecture and regulatory requirements, without exposing origins to the internet. Previously, CloudFront supported dual-stack for public origins but connected to VPC origins over IPv4 only. Customers faced a tradeoff: move origins to public subnets for IPv6 and give up VPC origin security or keep them private and stay on IPv4. Now, with this launch, customers can configure their VPC origins as dual-stack and get end-to-end IPv6 without sacrificing security. Dual-stack VPC origins are available in all AWS Commercial Regions where VPC origins are supported. The full list of supported Regions is available here . There is no additional cost for using dual-stack VPC origins. To learn more, visit CloudFront VPC origins.

title: Amazon Connect Customer now measures the outcomes that drive retention and revenue
body: Amazon Connect Customer now scores the outcome of your customer interactions. It shows whether the customer left satisfied, is at risk of churning, made a purchase, or resolved their need in self-service. You can now see whether an interaction worked, not just how efficiently it ran. Each metric comes with a default definition you can adjust to match how your business defines success and are available both through the analytics dashboards and APIs.

title: Amazon Connect Customer now prefills step-by-step guides for after contact work
body: Amazon Connect Customer can now fill in the step-by-step guides that agents complete after a contact, using information extracted from customer conversations, such as booking identifiers, claim numbers, and conversation summaries. Managers can set which information populates each form field. Agents can review and submit rather than manually typing in each field, saving time and improving data accuracy during after contact work. Contact center agents spend time after each contact entering frequently used information into a step-by-step guide. For example, an insurance agent who finishes a claims call might record the customer’s policy number, a summary of the call, and a disposition code. Now, managers can define rules for which information to extract from the conversation and which fields to automatically fill in the guide. The agent can then check the information, make any necessary corrections, and submit the guide, shortening after contact work and reducing data entry errors. You can use step-by-step guides with information extraction in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London). Contact summaries are also available in Africa (Cape Town). To learn more and get started, see step-by-step guides in the Amazon Connect Customer administrator guide.

title: AWS Deadline Cloud now helps users find their accessible resources in the Deadline Cloud monitor
body: AWS Deadline Cloud now lets users who have access to specific queues, fleets, or jobs, rather than an entire farm, find the resources they can reach directly from the Deadline Cloud monitor. Deadline Cloud is a fully managed service that helps teams run compute-intensive workloads for visual effects, animation, product design, simulation, and gaming. Previously, a user with access to only one queue had to get the farm ID from an administrator before they could reach their work. With this launch, the Deadline Cloud monitor displays to users queues they have access to, the parent IDs needed to reach them, and their level of access, covering both direct and group-inherited permissions. Teams now can share a single monitor entry point (URL) across different permission levels without additional coordination. Resource discovery is available in all AWS Regions where Deadline Cloud is available. To learn more, visit the AWS Deadline Cloud user guide .

title: AWS EC2 Auto Scaling now supports Launch Before Terminate at account-level to replace instances
body: AWS EC2 Auto Scaling now lets you enable Launch Before Terminate as the default replacement behavior across all Auto Scaling groups in your account. When enabled, Auto Scaling launches a replacement instance and waits for it to pass health checks before terminating the instance it replaces, helping your applications maintain full capacity and availability during instance replacement events. This applies to replacement events such as instance refreshes, rebalancing, health checks, and maximum-instance-lifetime replacements. You can enable Launch Before Terminate through AWS EC2 Auto Scaling account settings, which let you configure the behavior once at the account level instead of on each Auto Scaling group individually. You can manage the setting with the new `PutAccountSetting` and `DescribeAccountSettings` APIs, available through the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. Launch Before Terminate is available in all AWS Regions at no additional cost. To learn more, see Launch Before Terminate in the AWS EC2 Auto Scaling User Guide and AWS EC2 Auto Scaling API Reference Guide .

title: Amazon ECS adds LiveTaskCount and removes the charge for RunningTaskCount metric
body: Today, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) announces LiveTaskCount, a new ECS service metric that reports how many tasks are actively running in your service, available to all customers at no additional charge. Additionally, the existing RunningTaskCount metric in Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights no longer incurs a charge. LiveTaskCount reports the number of actively running ECS tasks across all desired states (ACTIVATING, RUNNING, and DEACTIVATING), including tasks still running while transitioning to a stopped state, for example, tasks undergoing connection draining during a scale-in event. This comprehensive state coverage makes LiveTaskCount well suited for autoscaling policies and capacity planning where a complete view of active, metric-generating tasks is required. It is available at no charge as part of ECS service utilization metrics and does not require opting in to CloudWatch Container Insights. The existing CloudWatch Container Insights RunningTaskCount metric tracks tasks where both the current and desired state are RUNNING, and continues to serve as a health and stability signal for customers who depend on it. With today's update, RunningTaskCount is now available at no additional charge for all CloudWatch Container Insights users. These updates are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon ECS is available. No action is required, and the pricing change for RunningTaskCount takes effect beginning October 1, 2026, and applies automatically. To learn more, see ECS CloudWatch metrics and ECS Container Insights metrics . For a pricing example, see Amazon CloudWatch pricing .

title: Serverless Storage on Amazon EMR Serverless now supports terabyte-scale shuffle
body: Amazon EMR Serverless now offers enhanced serverless storage capabilities with support for up to 1TB shuffle operations, raising the previous 200 GB per-job limit. Amazon EMR Serverless makes it simple for data engineers and data scientists to run open-source big data analytics frameworks without configuring, managing, and scaling clusters or servers. This enhancement enables enterprise customers to run production-scale Apache Spark workloads that require processing large volumes of shuffle data during complex operations such as joins, aggregations, and sorting. Enterprise data teams can now confidently migrate production workloads that routinely process terabyte-scale datasets without worrying about storage constraints. This enhancement is particularly valuable for workloads involving large table joins across multi-terabyte datasets, and complex aggregations on high-cardinality data that require extensive data shuffling. The addition of spill support ensures that jobs can seamlessly handle memory-intensive operations by offloading data to disk when necessary, improving job reliability and success rates for demanding analytical workloads. This feature is available with Amazon emr-7.14, emr-spark-8.1 and later, in 18 AWS Regions where Amazon EMR Serverless is available. See the Amazon EMR documentation for the full list of supported Regions and their applicable limits. To learn more about Amazon EMR Serverless and get started with terabyte-scale shuffle support, visit the Amazon EMR Serverless page .

title: Amazon GuardDuty RDS Protection now detects data exfiltration and destruction in Aurora and RDS databases
body: Amazon GuardDuty announces an expansion of RDS Protection that extends threat detection beyond login anomalies to identify data exfiltration and data destruction attacks targeting Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL databases. Available as RDS Protection for data activity, this new capability uses machine learning (ML)-based anomaly detection and integrated threat intelligence to continuously monitor database query patterns, helping you detect unusual data activity without requiring any agents, additional infrastructure, or database configuration changes. As attackers increasingly target databases to exfiltrate or destroy critical data after obtaining valid credentials through phishing, social engineering, or misconfiguration, their malicious database activity can appear indistinguishable from legitimate application behavior. RDS Protection for data activity establishes behavioral baselines for normal query patterns enabling GuardDuty to detect threats that traditional tools miss. You can enable GuardDuty RDS Protection for data activity as an add-on to RDS Protection for login activity. With a single click, they can enable it for their entire organization in the GuardDuty console, or programmatically via APIs, SDKs, CLI, or AWS CloudFormation. A 30-day free trial is available per account per Region. This feature is available today in all AWS commercial Regions and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, where Amazon GuardDuty RDS Protection is offered with support for Aurora PostgreSQL and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. For supported versions visit GuardDuty RDS Protection documentation . To learn more and start your free trial, visit the Amazon GuardDuty product page .

title: AWS Key Management Service now supports ML-KEM for post-quantum key encapsulation
body: AWS Key Management Service (KMS) now supports Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM), a post-quantum cryptography standard under NIST FIPS 203 , which enables two parties to establish a shared secret. NIST designed ML-KEM to replace the classical key-establishment schemes, like DH/ECDH key agreement, and RSA-based key transport, in their strategic cryptographic roadmap (see NIST IR 8547 ). ML-KEM addresses the "harvest now, decrypt later" threat to those classical schemes, where an adversary records the key-establishment exchange today and recovers the shared secret once sufficiently powerful quantum computers become available. KMS supports all three ML-KEM key specs defined in NIST FIPS 203: ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024. The Encapsulate API uses the public key to produce a random 32-byte shared secret and its ciphertext form. The Decapsulate API recovers the shared secret from ciphertext using the corresponding private key. KMS protects the private key of an ML-KEM key pair in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated hardware security modules (HSMs). You can use the GetPublicKey API to export the public key and distribute it to partners, client applications, or external systems for performing the encapsulate operation locally using cryptographic libraries like AWS-LC, OpenSSL, or Bouncy Castle. ML-KEM is available in all AWS Regions where KMS is available, except the the Middle East (UAE), Middle East (Bahrain), and China Regions. For more information, see ML-KEM keys in AWS KMS and Key spec reference in the AWS KMS Developer Guide.

title: Announcing the AWS Marketplace and Amazon Business unified storefront
body: Today, AWS Marketplace and Amazon Business announced the unified storefront. Organizations can now give their teams one curated catalog that puts software, data, and AI tools from AWS Marketplace alongside physical goods and supplies from Amazon Business. Many enterprises already buy from both, but they manage two catalogs with duplicated approval rules and separate reporting. The unified storefront can now give procurement teams one front door for both. Built on AWS Marketplace Storefront, the unified storefront lets administrators connect their organization's Amazon Business account and import Amazon Business products into their branded storefront. Administrators set governance rules once, and they apply across both catalogs. Buyers can browse AWS Marketplace listings and Amazon Business products in one place. Purchases of AWS Marketplace listings complete directly in the storefront and appear on the customer's AWS invoice. When a buyer selects an Amazon Business product, single sign-on takes them to an authenticated Amazon Business cart, so they don't need a second login. Each storefront connects only to the accounts its administrator sets up. The Amazon Business connector is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Marketplace operates to AWS Marketplace Storefront customers who have access to both the AWS Marketplace and Amazon Business APIs. To learn more, visit the AWS Marketplace Storefront product page and the AWS Marketplace Storefront User Guide .

title: SageMaker MLflow Apps now support MLflow 3.16
body: Amazon SageMaker AI MLflow Apps now support MLflow 3.16, bringing a redesigned tracing experience and faster experiment tracking to your generative AI and machine learning workflows. MLflow 3.16 improves debugging and analysis of generative AI applications and agents. The redesigned trace explorer is now the default, with adjustable row height, reorderable columns, custom columns from any trace tag or metadata field. This release also accelerates metric charts for experiments with large metric histories. New MLflow Apps are created on MLflow 3.16 by default. Existing MLflow Apps will be upgraded to MLflow 3.16 during an upcoming maintenance window, with no action required. MLflow 3.16 is available in all AWS Regions where MLflow Apps are available. To learn more, visit the SageMaker AI MLflow developer guide .

title: OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock
body: Today, AWS announces the general availability of OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra on Amazon Bedrock. GPT-6.1 Terra expands the GPT-6 family with a balance of capability, speed, and cost efficiency for everyday workloads. As the newest model in the Terra line, GPT-6.1 Terra combines detailed visual reasoning, accurate computer use, and improved factuality and natural writing over GPT-5.6 Terra, for complex workflows. In OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation, it scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra, performed on par with GPT-6 Astra, and completed tasks more than three times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. GPT-6.1 Terra offers balanced performance with input and output token prices at least 50% lower than those of GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It supports a context window of up to 1 million input tokens and accepts both text and image inputs. The Amazon Bedrock inference engine delivers the performance, security, and scale required for enterprise workloads. You can call GPT-6.1 Terra directly through Amazon Bedrock APIs or configure ChatGPT Work and Codex to use the model on Amazon Bedrock. Use it to draft proposals, interpret technical drawings, investigate codebases, and build agents that operate across business systems. Established AWS controls help you secure workloads, govern access, and audit model invocation activity. You can get started in the Amazon Bedrock console or programmatically through supported Amazon Bedrock APIs. For information about supported AWS Regions, endpoints, APIs, features, inference profiles and pricing, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation.

title: Amazon OpenSearch Service introduces validation advisory for domain configuration changes
body: Amazon OpenSearch Service now provides validation advisory for domain configuration changes, which helps you make informed decisions about changes that carry risk but can still be applied. Each configuration validation is now classified as either Critical, which blocks the change, or Warning, which gives advisory guidance that you can acknowledge before you proceed. Previously, validation results were limited to pass or block. There was no way to flag changes that would succeed but carry risk. Validation advisory helps you find potential issues without blocking deployments. Examples include dedicated coordinator nodes that may be too small for the data node configuration, or a shard count that exceeds the recommended limit for the cluster. You can acknowledge warnings when you first submit a change, review severity in dry-run results before applying changes, set acknowledgments directly in AWS CloudFormation templates, and see severity in API responses and Amazon EventBridge notifications. Validation advisory supports all Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running either OpenSearch or Elasticsearch versions. It is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon OpenSearch Service is available. To learn more, see the documentation .

title: Polly Generative engine upgraded with more natural speech, 14 new voices, and 2 new languages
body: Today, we are introducing a new model behind the Amazon Polly Generative engine that delivers more natural-sounding, accurate speech output with low latency. With this upgrade, you get access to an enhanced voice portfolio with higher overall quality, 14 new voices across nine locales, and two new languages—Hindi and Finnish—now generally available on the Generative engine for the first time. New voices include Kenneth and Nate (US English), Russell and Curtis (Australian English), Kiara and Arjun (Hindi and Indian English), Tina (German), Carlos (US Spanish), Leo and Carolina (Brazilian Portuguese), Hyunduk (Korean), and Suvi (Finnish). Amazon Polly is a fully managed service that turns text into natural-sounding speech. This drop-in model upgrade makes Generative voices more natural and accurate. Complex content such as numbers, email addresses, and street addresses is designed to sound more reliable, reducing the need to fine-tune speech output. You can continue to use Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) tags to control speech output on the Generative engine, just as before. The low-latency streaming API makes it easy to build contact center experiences, chatbots, and large language model (LLM) based agentic voice applications for real-time conversations. The richness and variety of voice options are also well suited for news, media, entertainment, e-learning, and accessibility use cases. This launch also expands the Amazon Polly Generative offering to AWS GovCloud, providing more options for public sector and regulated industries. All new Generative voices are now available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Zurich), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). To hear how Polly voices sound, go to Amazon Polly Features . For more details on the Polly offerings and use, see the Amazon Polly documentation and pricing page .

title: Amazon RDS Proxy now supports SQL Server 2022
body: Amazon RDS Proxy , a fully managed, highly available database proxy for Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS) , now supports Amazon RDS for SQL Server instances running major version 2022. Amazon RDS Proxy sits between your application and the database to pool and share established database connections, improving database efficiency and application scalability. For Amazon RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ databases, RDS Proxy automatically connects to the standby database instance during a failure, preserves application connections, and helps reduce failover times by up to 83%. RDS Proxy supports standard IAM authentication for SQL Server, where your applications authenticate to the proxy using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and RDS Proxy manages database connections using credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager. You can enable Amazon RDS Proxy for your SQL Server 2022 database in a few steps on the Amazon RDS console, then connect by pointing your application to the RDS Proxy endpoint. To get started, see our documentation .

title: Amazon Redshift adds support for creating and refreshing Apache Iceberg materialized views
body: Amazon Redshift now supports the creation and refresh of Apache Iceberg materialized views. Materialized views pre-compute expensive joins and aggregations once and store the results in an Apache Iceberg table in Amazon S3 or Amazon S3 table buckets, registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Materialized views are created using familiar SQL — CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... USING ICEBERG and the results are instantly queryable by any Iceberg-compatible engine, including Amazon Athena, Apache Spark on Amazon EMR and AWS Glue, and third-party engines such as Trino, or Snowflake. Redshift keeps them current by recomputing only what has changed with manual incremental refresh, and because the results are Iceberg tables in the Glue Data Catalog, they are governed and discovered like any other catalog table. Data teams often build analytics in stages, stitching together different engines to clean and transform raw data before serving it. This adds pipeline orchestration overhead and can introduce semantic differences between engines. Iceberg materialized views deliver value in two ways. First, instead of hundreds of users and teams re-running the same expensive joins and aggregations, and re-scanning source tables on every query, you compute the result once and everyone reads the precomputed table. Second, you can run an end-to-end pipeline using a single engine like Apache Spark and now Amazon Redshift, and every downstream consumer shares the same open result without the overhead of orchestrating multiple engines. Either way, the output is an open Iceberg table that any engine can read without copies or conversion. You can still load these tables into Redshift Managed Storage (RMS) as native RMS materialized views for your most performance-sensitive dashboards. You can create Iceberg Materialized Views in any region where Redshift Serverless and provisioned Graviton instances are supported. To learn more, see Materialized views stored as Apache Iceberg tables in the Amazon Redshift Database Developer Guide, the CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW command reference, and the Materialize once, query anywhere blog post.

title: Announcing DNS analytics and insights for Route 53 Global Resolver and DNS Firewall
body: Route 53 Global Resolver and DNS Firewall now provide DNS analytics and insights through native Amazon CloudWatch integration. These new capabilities enable network administrators and security teams to gain full observability into DNS query patterns, monitor DNS Firewall rule effectiveness, detect anomalous activity, and optimize DNS infrastructure performance. DNS analytics and insights is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon CloudWatch, Route 53 Global Resolver, and DNS Firewall are available. With CloudWatch Metrics and Contributor Insights, customers can search and analyze DNS query logs, create metric filters for specific patterns such as blocked queries and DNS response codes, and set automated alarms. A new Analytics tab in both the Global Resolver and DNS Firewall consoles provides streamlined access to all analytics in one place. For example, customers can create a metric filter for blocked DNS queries by VPC and set an alarm to trigger when more than 10 queries are blocked within an hour, enabling rapid response to potential security threats. Standard Amazon CloudWatch pricing applies to the metrics that customers opt in to. To learn more, visit the Route 53 documentation .

title: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio now supports custom Tooling blueprints
body: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio now supports custom Tooling blueprints, giving domain administrators the ability to define the foundation of every project by using their own AWS CloudFormation templates. Administrators can tailor project environments to meet organization-specific requirements, such as IAM role names that comply with company naming standards or custom permissions boundaries instead of AWS managed policies. Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio administrators start by authoring a CloudFormation template that describes the project environment they need, then register it as a custom Tooling blueprint. The service validates the template at registration and again after each project deployment, confirming that the required resources exist before any team member uses the project. Templates can include any CloudFormation-supported resource, such as AWS Lake Formation grants, Amazon Athena workgroups, or VPC security groups, and work across multiple AWS accounts and Regions without per-project edits. At deployment time, the service automatically populates reserved template parameters, such as the project ID and domain ID, so administrators define the template once and apply it everywhere. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio is available. To learn more, visit the Custom blueprints as Tooling documentation .

title: AWS Security Hub CSPM now supports the Cyber Risk Institute profile version 2.2
body: AWS Security Hub CSPM now supports automated security checks that align with the Cyber Risk Institute (CRI) profile. The CRI Profile is a cybersecurity framework developed by the Cyber Risk Institute, a non-profit coalition of financial institutions and trade associations. The framework harmonizes cybersecurity and regulatory expectations that apply to the financial services sector into a common set of requirements, so that an organization can assess itself once and report against multiple regulations. AWS Security Hub CSPM provides 404 controls that support a subset of CRI Profile v2.2 requirements; the controls don't support requirements that require manual checks. The new standard is now available in all AWS Regions where Security Hub CSPM is currently available, including the AWS GovCloud (US) and the China Regions. To quickly enable the standard across your AWS environment, we recommend that you use Security Hub central configuration. With this approach, you can enable the standard in all or only some of your organization's accounts and across all AWS Regions that are linked to Security Hub with a single action. To learn more, see CRI Profile v2.2 in the AWS Security Hub CSPM user guide. To receive notifications about new Security Hub CSPM features and controls subscribe to the Security Hub SNS topic . You can also try Security Hub CSPM at no cost for 30 days with the AWS Free Tier offering.

title: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio adds light mode support for IDC-based domains
body: Today, AWS announces light mode support in Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio for Identity Center (IDC) based domains. Customers can now configure the visual interface mode to match their preference, choosing between dark and light themes. With this launch, customers can set this visual preference in both IAM-based and IDC-based domains. Light mode helps improve readability in bright environments and provides a familiar visual experience for customers who prefer lighter interfaces. Combined with the existing dark mode, this update gives you full control over the appearance of your development environment, improving accessibility and reducing eye strain across varying lighting conditions. In SageMaker Unified Studio settings, you can choose 'Customize appearance' under your Profile settings to select between visual modes including dark mode, light mode, and device setting, which matches your operating system's setting. The setting persists across browsers and devices. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio is available. To learn more, see the Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio User Guide.

title: Introducing time series collections for the next generation of Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
body: Today, we're announcing support for time series collections on the next generation of Amazon OpenSearch Serverless. With time series collections, you can ingest, store, and analyze logs, metrics, traces, and event data without provisioning or managing clusters. They absorb ingest spikes automatically, keep recent data fast to query, and make months or years of history searchable at low cost, all in the same collection. Time series collections add a new, lower-cost warm storage tier in addition to the existing hot storage tier, so customers can retain their infrequently accessed data without paying hot storage prices. Customers can choose how long data stays hot before transitiong to warm storage. With up to 100 TB of hot storage per collection, time series collections can handle high-volume observability workloads such as application monitoring, security analytics, and IoT telemetry. Alerting and anomaly detection are also now available, so customers can get notified about issues and spot unusual patterns in their log and event data without separate tooling. Time series collections are available today in all AWS Regions where OpenSearch Serverless is available. To learn more about the pricing for the new warm storage, see OpenSearch Serverless pricing . To learn more about time series collections on Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, see the OpenSearch Serverless feature page , the launch blog , and the AWS documentation .

title: AWS Transfer Family console supports SVG logos and ICO favicons for web apps
body: The AWS Transfer Family console now supports SVG files for logos and ICO files for favicons in web apps, with upload limits increased to 2 MB. This gives you more flexibility to use existing branding assets when customizing your web app. Previously, the console accepted only JPG and PNG files and limited logo uploads to 50 KB and favicon uploads to 20 KB. The console automatically resizes images and converts them to JPG or PNG before saving them. Existing API upload limits and format requirements remain unchanged. These capabilities are available in all AWS Regions where Transfer Family web apps are offered. To learn more, see the Transfer Family web apps tutorial .

title: Amazon WorkSpaces simplifies secure AI agent access to enterprise cloud desktops with less infrastructure to operate and manage
body: WorkSpaces for AI agents now handles authentication and desktop connections as part of the managed Model Context Protocol (MCP) service, so you can connect agents to governed cloud desktops, removing the need to write custom code. This makes it easy to use WorkSpaces with any client that supports MCP. Connecting an agent to a desktop previously required you to manage presession requirements; generate, invoke, and rotate streaming URLs manually, adding complexity every time a session expired.
